comparedAgainst: https://martinfowler.com/articles/mocksArentStubs.html — Fowler, "Mocks Aren't Stubs": the canonical top-ranking page for this query. Fetched and checked verbatim: the dummy/fake/stub/spy/mock definitions and the 'only mocks insist upon behavior verification' line match the article's paraphrase exactly, with no close copying. Fowler's piece has no runnable code, no C#, and no exercises; this article goes deeper (five hand-rolled kinds against one program, a working library comparison, an empirical over-mocking demonstration with real PASS/FAIL output) while staying at least as accurate.

justification: No factual error found after re-deriving the code and fetching every cited primary source. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/testing/test-doubles.md` reports PASS (blocks=22, executed=4); I independently re-traced all four executed programs by hand, including the subtlest one (the strict-mock Script in the over-mocking section): Gate A calls tickets.Find, then clock.Now, then terminal.Charge, then tickets.Save, in that exact order, matching the script and passing; Gate B reads clock.Now first, so its first call is clock.Now against an expected tickets.Find T-17, which correctly reproduces the article's shown failure message ('call 1 was clock.Now / expected tickets.Find T-17'); Gate C never calls tickets.Save, correctly reproducing both the state-based failure (exit time null) and the mock failure (never received tickets.Save T-17). Tariff math (160 minutes = 3 started hours = 6.00) is correct. No code block references xUnit or any package other than NSubstitute 5.3.0 (issue #12 does not apply; not a blocker). Every checkable citation was fetched and holds up: Fowler's dummy/fake/stub/spy/mock definitions and 'only mocks insist on behavior verification' (Mocks Aren't Stubs); the xUnit Test Patterns chapter titles and contents exactly match the publisher's own listing at informit.com (ch. 11 'Using Test Doubles' covering indirect inputs/outputs, ch. 23 'Test Double Patterns' with Test Stub/Test Spy/Mock Object/Fake Object as its pattern entries, ch. 27 'Value Patterns' with Dummy Object) — a pre-publication Library of Congress CIP record shows different working titles ('Test Double Usage Patterns', 'Attribute Value Patterns'), but that record is superseded by the published book's own table of contents, which is what the article cites and matches; xunitpatterns.com's Test Double page does say a doubled configuration is never run in production and that at least one test should verify the real assembly, matching the article's closing paragraph; the Microsoft Learn unit-testing-best-practices page's own note ('Fowler and Meszaros... use these words more narrowly: a stub provides data, a mock verifies interactions, and a fake is a working alternative implementation') matches the article's summary of it precisely, including that fake is Microsoft's umbrella term and mock/stub are separated only by whether the test asserts against the double; NSubstitute's getting-started page contains the near-verbatim line the article paraphrases about not bothering to name stub/mock/fake/spy; NSubstitute's received-calls page confirms ReceivedCallsException lists actual vs. expected calls; Moq's Quickstart confirms loose-by-default behavior and MockBehavior.Strict; the File-based apps doc confirms native AOT publishing is on by default for file-based apps and that `#:property PublishAot=false` is the documented way to turn it off, exactly as used in the NSubstitute program; the TimeProvider overview confirms TimeProvider is a .NET 8+ abstraction with TimeProvider.System as the real implementation, FakeTimeProvider in Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing, and Task.Delay/CancellationTokenSource overloads accepting a TimeProvider; Software Engineering at Google ch. 13 confirms the 'prefer a real implementation when fast and deterministic' rule, fidelity and contract-test language, and the state-changing-vs-query rule of thumb for interaction testing, all reproduced accurately. Against the best-ranking pages for this query, the article is clearly ahead: it is the only one of the four compared pages that hand-rolls all five Meszaros kinds against a single running C# program, shows what a mocking library (NSubstitute) actually generates versus what it can't (a fake), and then proves the over-mocking claim empirically (a behavior-preserving refactor breaks a strict mock test but not a state-based one, with real captured output) rather than asserting it. The one thing keeping this off a 10: the 'Why .NET code calls everything a mock' section states flatly that under Microsoft's terminology 'InMemoryTicketStore has no special name,' but by Microsoft's own rule (asserted-against = mock) the store is asserted against directly in the 'stub: declined card' test (`Check.Equal(null, store.Find("T-17")!.Exited)`), so under that same rule it would be called a mock in that test — the sentence is defensible as shorthand for 'Microsoft's scheme has no name for the fake pattern itself,' but as written it reads as a stronger, slightly imprecise claim than the source supports. That is a clarity nit, not a factual error, so it does not cap the score, but it keeps this at 9.0 rather than higher.

issues.location: "Why .NET code calls everything a mock" section, the sentence "Under that definition this article's `SpyTerminal` is a mock, and `InMemoryTicketStore` has no special name."
issues.problem: Microsoft's rule (per the cited page) is that a fake becomes a mock the moment a test asserts against it, and not otherwise a stub. `InMemoryTicketStore` is asserted against directly in the earlier 'stub: declined card' test (`Check.Equal(null, store.Find("T-17")!.Exited)`), so by that same rule it would be a mock in that test — it isn't correct to say it categorically 'has no special name' under Microsoft's terminology; its Microsoft-name, like `SpyTerminal`'s, depends on which test is asking, exactly as the article's own 'kind is a role, not a property of a class' point (stated two sections earlier) would predict.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either pick a specific test to anchor the claim ('...and in the fake test, where nothing is asserted against the store, `InMemoryTicketStore` would just be a stub') or soften to what is actually true: Microsoft's two-role scheme has no separate name for the *fake* pattern itself (a working shortcut implementation), so it always collapses into mock-or-stub depending on the test, unlike Meszaros's taxonomy which gives it its own kind.
